newsitem.title: USA: Mortgage rates rise in week.
newsitem.headline: Mortgage rates rise in week.

text.p: Interest rates on home mortgages rose this week on concern over stronger inflation, the Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp. said Thursday.

The average rate on 30-year fixed-rate mortgages rose to 7.57 percent in the week ending Dec. 13 after falling for seven consecutive weeks, it said. Last week, rates on 30-year fixed rate loans were at 7.44 percent.
Fifteen-year loans also rose, to an average 7.06 percent in the week after falling seven consecutive weeks. Last week's 15-year rate averaged 6.96 percent.
Adjustable rate mortgages inched upward to an average 5.52 percent from 5.47 percent last week, Freddie Mac said.

"This week's release of the consumer and producer price indices for the month of November showed the producer price index rising four tenths of a percent, which made the market a little nervous about inflation and pushed interest rates up slightly," said Frank Nothaft, Freddie Mac deputy chief economist.
A year ago, the 30-year rate averaged 7.15 percent, the 15-year was at 6.71 percent and the ARM was at 5.55 percent.
Earlier Thursday the Labour Department said November consumer prices rose 0.3 percent, but excluding food and energy were up only 0.2 percent.
The department said Wednesday that producer prices excluding food and energy fell 0.3 percent last month.
The Labour Department also reported a 118,000 increase in November non-farm payrolls and a jobless rate of 5.4 percent.

Freddie Mac said lenders charged an average 1.7 percent in fees and points on 30- and 15-year loans, both unchanged from last week. They charged 1.4 percent on adjustable loans, up from 1.3 percent the prior week.
